title: True Random Number Generators (TRNG): Phase Jitter, Thermal Shot Noise & Metastability Entropy Harvesters
goal: Master the physics, architectures, and defenses of hardware True Random Number Generators (TRNG), including Johnson-Nyquist thermal noise, Ring Oscillator phase jitter sampling, metastability latches, Von Neumann de-biasing, and NIST SP 800-90B active health tests.
recap: Yesterday in Day 47, we solved the noisy silicon channel problem using Fuzzy Extractors and BCH error-correcting codes to derive static keys. Today, we conquer dynamic entropy by designing hardware True Random Number Generators that harvest quantum thermal noise and phase jitter for unpredictable cryptographic operations.

parts.title: Physics of Hardware Randomness: Johnson-Nyquist Thermal Noise & Quantum Shot Noise
say: Welcome to Day 48 of Course 19: Advanced IoT Hardware Security, Root of Trust & Quantum-Resilient Silicon. Over the preceding two days, we harnessed semiconductor manufacturing imperfections to build Physical Unclonable Functions--static physical fingerprints that reconstitute immutable cryptographic master keys. Today, we turn our architectural attention to the complementary foundational primitive in silicon security: the True Random Number Generator (TRNG). While a PUF provides static, repeatable device identity, a TRNG provides fresh, non-deterministic, irreproducible entropy on every single clock cycle. Every non-deterministic cryptographic protocol--including ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchanges (ECDH), digital signature nonces (ECDSA/Ed25519), initialization vectors (AES-GCM), and cryptographic salts--relies unconditionally on the cryptographic unpredictability of the TRNG. If an adversary can bias, predict, or manipulate the random number generator, the entire cryptographic citadel collapses regardless of key length.

Unlike Pseudo-Random Number Generators (PRNGs) or Deterministic Random Bit Generators (DRBGs), which expand a deterministic secret seed via mathematical algorithms (such as AES-CTR-DRBG or Hash-DRBG), a True Random Number Generator extracts entropy directly from unpredictable microscopic physical phenomena occurring inside the electronic hardware. Understanding these physical entropy sources requires deep immersion into quantum mechanics and semiconductor physics.

The first ubiquitous physical entropy source is Thermal Noise (also known as Johnson-Nyquist Noise). Thermal noise arises from the agitated, stochastic Brownian motion of charge carriers (free electrons) inside an electrical conductor or semiconductor resistor, even in the complete absence of an applied external electric field. According to the Nyquist-Johnson formula, the root-mean-square (RMS) thermal noise voltage spectral density across a resistance R over bandwidth Delta_f at absolute temperature T is given by: V_rms = sqrt(4 * k_B * T * R * Delta_f), where k_B is Boltzmann's constant (1.380649e-23 J/K). Because thermal agitation is driven by thermodynamic microscopic fluctuations, thermal noise exhibits an ideal Gaussian distribution with zero correlation across time, providing a pristine, quantum-mechanical entropy baseline.

The second vital physical mechanism is Shot Noise. Unlike thermal noise, which occurs in equilibrium conductors, shot noise is fundamentally tied to the quantum discreteness of electrical charge. When electrical current flows across a potential barrier--such as a p-n junction, a Zener diode operating in avalanche breakdown, or the microscopic gate dielectric barrier of a MOSFET undergoing quantum Fowler-Nordheim tunneling--the electric current is not a continuous fluid. Instead, it consists of individual discrete electrons carrying charge q = 1.602e-19 Coulombs traversing the barrier stochastically governed by Poisson arrival statistics. The RMS shot noise current across bandwidth Delta_f is: I_rms = sqrt(2 * q * I_dc * Delta_f), where I_dc is the average DC current.

A third physical noise phenomenon present in semiconductor devices is Flicker Noise (or 1/f Pink Noise). In sub-micron MOSFETs, flicker noise is generated by the random capture and release of conduction carriers at defect traps located at the silicon-dielectric interface (governed by McWhorter's surface state trapping model). While flicker noise dominates low-frequency domains (below 100 kHz), hardware security architects intentionally design high-frequency noise harvesting amplifiers that operate in the megahertz and gigahertz regimes. By filtering out low-frequency 1/f noise, the TRNG samples purely white, delta-correlated thermal and shot noise spectra.

Quantum tunneling through ultra-thin oxide barriers provides another pristine source of non-determinism. Under the quantum Fowler-Nordheim tunneling model, the probability P of a valence electron penetrating through a triangular potential barrier of height Phi_B under an electric field E is governed by the WKB approximation: P proportional to exp(-4 * sqrt(2*m*) * Phi_B^(3/2) / (3 * q * hbar * E)). Because wave function collapse is non-deterministic at the quantum level, quantum tunneling noise represents an unassailable physical entropy source.

Hardware security architects classify TRNGs under international security standards such as NIST SP 800-90B, BSI AIS-31 (Class PTG.2 / PTG.3), and ISO/IEC 18031. These standards mandate that a true physical entropy source must be isolated from deterministic digital noise, continuously monitored by dedicated hardware health-test circuits, and mathematically characterized to guarantee a certified min-entropy lower bound.

Today, we will analyze, model, and implement the complete TRNG hardware stack: physical noise harvesters, ring oscillator phase-jitter sampling, metastability resolving latches, Von Neumann de-biasing, and active anti-manipulation circuit defenses.

# Day 48 Part 1: Physical Entropy Sources: Johnson-Nyquist Thermal Noise & Shot Noise Simulation
import struct
import math
import random

class PhysicalEntropyPhysicsModel:
    """Simulates microscopic thermal Johnson-Nyquist noise and quantum shot noise."""
    def __init__(self, resistance_ohms: float = 10000.0, bandwidth_hz: float = 1.0e6, temp_kelvin: float = 300.0):
        self.k_B = 1.380649e-23  # Boltzmann's constant in J/K
        self.q = 1.60217663e-19   # Elementary electron charge in Coulombs
        self.r = resistance_ohms
        self.bw = bandwidth_hz
        self.temp = temp_kelvin

        # Theoretical RMS Johnson-Nyquist thermal noise: V_rms = sqrt(4 * k_B * T * R * Delta_f)
        self.v_thermal_rms = math.sqrt(4.0 * self.k_B * self.temp * self.r * self.bw)

    def sample_thermal_voltage(self) -> float:
        """Samples instantaneous analog thermal noise voltage (Volts)."""
        return random.gauss(0.0, self.v_thermal_rms)

    def calculate_shot_noise_current(self, dc_current_amps: float = 1.0e-3) -> dict:
        """Calculates quantum Poisson shot noise across semiconductor junction."""
        # I_rms = sqrt(2 * q * I_dc * Delta_f)
        i_shot_rms = math.sqrt(2.0 * self.q * dc_current_amps * self.bw)
        # Ratio of shot noise to DC signal (noise-to-signal ratio)
        nsr = (i_shot_rms / dc_current_amps) * 100.0
        return {
            'dc_current_ma': dc_current_amps * 1000.0,
            'shot_noise_rms_na': i_shot_rms * 1.0e9,
            'noise_to_signal_pct': round(nsr, 4)
        }

def run_physical_entropy_demonstration():
    random.seed(0x5EED4801)
    model = PhysicalEntropyPhysicsModel(resistance_ohms=10000.0, bandwidth_hz=10.0e6, temp_kelvin=300.0)
    print("=== Physical Entropy Harvest Physics (Thermal & Shot Noise) ===")
    print(f"Resistor: {model.r:.0f} Ohms | Bandwidth: {model.bw/1e6:.1f} MHz | Temp: {model.temp:.1f} K")
    print(f"Theoretical Thermal V_rms: {model.v_thermal_rms * 1.0e6:.3f} uV RMS\n")

    # Sample 5 discrete thermal voltage instances
    samples = [model.sample_thermal_voltage() * 1.0e6 for _ in range(5)]
    for idx, v in enumerate(samples):
        print(f"Sample {idx}: Analog Thermal Noise = {v:+7.3f} uV")

    # Shot noise characterization across reverse-biased junction
    shot = model.calculate_shot_noise_current(dc_current_amps=0.5e-3)
    print(f"\nReverse-Biased Diode Junction Shot Noise (I_dc = {shot['dc_current_ma']} mA):")
    print(f"Quantum Shot Noise Current: {shot['shot_noise_rms_na']:.2f} nA RMS")
    print("Physical Entropy Harvesting: INTRINSIC_QUANTUM_DISORDER_CONFIRMED")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    run_physical_entropy_demonstration()

parts.title: Ring Oscillator (RO) TRNG & Phase Jitter Sampling Dynamics
say: While discrete analog components--such as Zener breakdown diodes or low-noise analog operational amplifiers--provide rich thermal noise, integrating custom analog amplifiers onto a high-volume, digital CMOS system-on-chip or a standard FPGA is economically costly and layout-intensive. Consequently, the overwhelmingly dominant architecture for embedded TRNGs is the Ring Oscillator (RO) TRNG, which harvests phase jitter using purely digital standard logic cells.

In Day 46, we studied Ring Oscillators in the context of PUFs, where static, time-invariant manufacturing mismatch was the target signal, and temporal phase jitter was an unwanted noise source. In TRNG design, the architectural perspective flips entirely: the static process mismatch is an unwanted systematic bias, and temporal phase jitter (the dynamic timing noise) is the precious cryptographic entropy we wish to harvest!

Consider a high-frequency free-running Ring Oscillator (RO_fast) composed of an odd number of inverters (e.g., 3 or 5 stages), oscillating at 1.2 GHz. The period of oscillation T_osc is nominally fixed: T_nom = 1 / f_nom. However, on every single cycle of oscillation, microscopic thermal noise in the transistor channels perturbs the exact threshold switching moment, introducing a tiny temporal variance sigma_jitter (typically 1 to 5 picoseconds per cycle).

Because phase jitter is accumulated cycle-by-cycle as an unconstrained random walk, the total temporal uncertainty of the oscillator edge after k cycles scales proportionally to the square root of time: sigma_total(k) = sigma_jitter * sqrt(k). If we let the oscillator run for thousands of cycles, the accumulated edge uncertainty expands until it becomes larger than the entire period T_osc of the high-frequency oscillator! At that moment, the instantaneous phase of the high-frequency ring oscillator is completely random and uniformly distributed over the interval [0, 2*pi).

The canonical sampling architecture pairs this high-frequency ring oscillator with a slow, stable reference clock (CLK_slow, e.g., 25 MHz from an external crystal oscillator) driving a D flip-flop. The high-frequency RO signal is fed into the D input, while the slow reference clock clocks the flip-flop. At every rising edge of CLK_slow, the flip-flop samples whether the high-frequency RO is currently high ('1') or low ('0').

To maximize entropy per sampled bit, modern architectures use multiple independent Ring Oscillators (e.g., 16 or 32 ROs) running in parallel, with their outputs XORed together before sampling. By combining k independent jittery oscillators through an XOR tree, the transition edge density increases, and the effective entropy rate scales according to the XOR lemma: the bias of the XOR sum decreases exponentially with the number of independent entropy sources.

In high-speed FPGA and ASIC syntheses, physical layout engineers must carefully match the path delays across the XOR reduction tree. If path lengths through the XOR tree are unbalanced, high-frequency transition glitches (narrow hazard pulses of 50-100 ps) can propagate to the sampler, creating deterministic correlation patterns. To prevent glitch-induced bias, modern secure designs insert pipeline registers at each level of the XOR tree or utilize dual-rail differential logic.

Furthermore, hardware designers must protect RO-TRNGs against injection locking. If an attacker injects a strong external radio-frequency (RF) field or modulates the power supply voltage at the RO's natural resonance frequency, the ring oscillator can be forced to lock its phase to the external signal, collapsing entropy to zero. Implementing differential ring oscillators with spread-spectrum frequency jitter, prime-number inverter chain lengths (e.g., 5, 7, 11, 13 stages), and on-chip substrate shielding is mandatory in military and banking-grade security processors.

Another vital microarchitectural technique is Coherent Sampling vs Incoherent Sampling. If the sampling clock frequency f_sample is a rational fraction of the ring oscillator frequency f_RO (such that f_RO / f_sample = p / q for small integers p and q), the sampling edges fall into a repeating, deterministic periodic orbit. When this occurs, the sampled bits exhibit strong cyclic patterns even if jitter is present. To prevent harmonic lock, modern security architectures modulate the sampling frequency dynamically using an on-chip pseudo-random clock divider, ensuring that the phase trajectory remains strictly ergodic and aperiodic across the entire state space.

Silicon engineers also perform Jitter Spectral Density characterization during post-silicon validation. By connecting high-bandwidth on-chip digitizers to the ring oscillator output, engineers measure the phase noise spectrum L(f) in dBc/Hz across offset frequencies from 10 kHz to 100 MHz. Integrating the phase noise over this offset band yields the exact cycle-to-cycle RMS timing jitter: sigma_jitter = sqrt(2 * integral(10^(L(f)/10) df)) / (2 * pi * f_0). This empirical measurement validates that the harvested entropy originates from physical quantum thermal agitation rather than deterministic clock distribution artifacts.
parts.example: In a free-running ring oscillator, thermal noise causes edge timing to drift as a random walk (sigma proportional to sqrt(cycles)); sampling high-frequency ROs with a reference clock harvests true digital entropy.
parts.code:
# Day 48 Part 2: Ring Oscillator Phase Jitter Accumulation & D-Latch Sampling Simulator
import struct
import math
import random

class JitteryRingOscillator:
    """Simulates a high-frequency free-running ring oscillator with cycle-to-cycle phase jitter."""
    def __init__(self, ro_id: int, nominal_freq_hz: float = 1.0e9, cycle_jitter_ps: float = 3.5):
        self.ro_id = ro_id
        self.nominal_period_s = 1.0 / nominal_freq_hz
        self.jitter_sigma_s = cycle_jitter_ps * 1.0e-12
        self.current_time_s = 0.0

    def advance_to_timestamp(self, target_time_s: float) -> int:
        """Accumulates jitter steps until target timestamp and returns instantaneous digital state (0 or 1)."""
        while self.current_time_s < target_time_s:
            # Each half-cycle has nominal duration + Gaussian edge jitter
            half_period = (self.nominal_period_s / 2.0) + random.gauss(0.0, self.jitter_sigma_s)
            self.current_time_s += max(1.0e-13, half_period)
        
        # Determine instantaneous phase state: alternate high/low
        cycle_count = int(self.current_time_s / (self.nominal_period_s / 2.0))
        return cycle_count % 2

class RingOscillatorTRNG:
    """Multi-RO TRNG: XORs 8 independent jittery ring oscillators and samples with slow clock."""
    def __init__(self, num_ros: int = 8, sample_clock_hz: float = 25.0e6):
        self.num_ros = num_ros
        self.ros = [JitteryRingOscillator(i, nominal_freq_hz=1.0e9 + i*1.2e7, cycle_jitter_ps=3.0) for i in range(num_ros)]
        self.sample_period_s = 1.0 / sample_clock_hz
        self.global_clock_time = 0.0

    def sample_raw_bit(self) -> int:
        """Advances global clock by one sample cycle, samples all ROs, and XORs outputs."""
        self.global_clock_time += self.sample_period_s
        xor_result = 0
        for ro in self.ros:
            bit = ro.advance_to_timestamp(self.global_clock_time)
            xor_result ^= bit
        return xor_result

    def generate_raw_bitstream(self, num_bits: int = 64) -> str:
        """Harvests a sequence of raw unconditioned entropy bits."""
        return "".join(str(self.sample_raw_bit()) for _ in range(num_bits))

def run_ro_trng_simulation():
    random.seed(0x5EED4802)
    trng = RingOscillatorTRNG(num_ros=8, sample_clock_hz=25.0e6)
    print("=== Multi-Ring Oscillator Phase Jitter TRNG Harvesting ===")
    print(f"Oscillator Array: 8 Jittery Inverter Chains (~1.0 GHz)")
    print(f"Sampling Clock:   25.0 MHz Reference (Sampling Interval: 40 ns)")
    
    raw_stream = trng.generate_raw_bitstream(64)
    print(f"\nHarvested Raw Bitstream (64 bits):\n{raw_stream}")

    ones_count = raw_stream.count('1')
    zeros_count = raw_stream.count('0')
    print(f"\nRaw Bitstream Statistics:")
    print(f"Ones Count:  {ones_count} ({ones_count*100.0/len(raw_stream):.1f}%)")
    print(f"Zeros Count: {zeros_count} ({zeros_count*100.0/len(raw_stream):.1f}%)")
    print("RO-TRNG Status: JITTER_SAMPLING_ACTIVE")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    run_ro_trng_simulation()

parts.title: Metastability Entropy Sources: Cross-Coupled Inverter Saddle Point Contention
say: While phase-jitter ring oscillators accumulate timing uncertainty across many cycles, another powerful physical entropy mechanism operates within a single clock transition: Digital Metastability.

In digital electronics, bistable storage elements (such as D flip-flops, Set-Reset latches, and cross-coupled inverters) possess two stable states: logic 0 and logic 1. However, between these two stable attractors lies an unstable equilibrium point known as the Metastable State. If a flip-flop's setup and hold timing constraints are violated simultaneously--such that the data input transitions precisely during the clock aperture window--the cross-coupled feedback loop enters metastability, with both internal nodes hovering around Vdd / 2.

In traditional digital logic design, metastability is an engineer's worst nightmare, causing asynchronous clock domain crossing (CDC) failures and system crashes. But in hardware security, metastability is intentionally provoked and harvested as an ultra-high-speed physical entropy source!

Consider a Metastability-Based TRNG cell consisting of two cross-coupled NAND or NOR gates driven by balanced pre-charge and evaluate control signals. During the pre-charge phase (CLK = 0), both internal nodes Q and Q_bar are pulled equally to supply voltage Vdd (or ground). During the evaluate phase (CLK = 1), the pre-charge transistors are released, and the cross-coupled inverters are connected simultaneously.

The circuit attempts to resolve from this unstable saddle point. In the ideal mathematical world of zero noise and perfect circuit symmetry, the circuit would remain stuck at the saddle point forever. In physical silicon, microscopic thermal noise (Brownian electron motion in the transistor channels) creates an instantaneous millivolt potential differential across the nodes. The positive feedback loop amplifies this microscopic thermal difference exponentially: V_diff(t) = V_noise * exp(t / tau), where tau is the circuit's regeneration time constant.

Eventually, the differential exceeds the digital threshold, and the cell collapses into either State 0 or State 1. Crucially, the decision of whether the cell resolves to 0 or 1 is dictated entirely by the sign of the instantaneous thermal noise at the exact moment of evaluation. Furthermore, the resolving time T_resolve (the time required to escape metastability) is itself a random variable governed by: T_resolve = tau * ln(V_threshold / |V_noise|). Because thermal noise |V_noise| exhibits a Gaussian distribution, the resolving latency follows an exponential distribution.

To ensure that the latch is not systematically biased by static transistor mismatch (which would cause the latch to consistently resolve in one direction), hardware architects implement Active Offset Calibration. A small binary-weighted capacitive DAC (CDAC) or an array of digital trim transistors is connected to the internal storage nodes. During an automated startup calibration routine, a digital tracking loop adjusts the trim capacitance until the latch yields an exact 50.0% split between 0s and 1s over 10,000 trials.

In addition to binary state extraction, measuring the resolving time T_resolve provides a rich continuous entropy source. Because resolving latency follows an exponential tail distribution, a high-speed Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) composed of a tapped delay line of Vernier inverters can quantize T_resolve with sub-10-picosecond resolution. The least significant bits (LSBs) of the TDC measurement represent pure physical entropy that is uncorrelated with the binary resolution state, effectively doubling the entropy harvest rate of the latch cell.

Silicon validation engineers also monitor the latch for Memory Effect (or Hysteresis). If a metastable latch is evaluated repeatedly at extremely high clock frequencies (e.g. 500 MHz), residual trapped charge in the transistor gate oxide from the previous resolution cycle can bias the subsequent evaluation. To eliminate inter-cycle memory effects, industrial latch designs enforce a forced symmetric discharge phase between consecutive evaluations, grounding both internal nodes for a complete clock cycle to wipe out all remnant capacitive memory before entering the next pre-charge phase.

Hardware architects can harvest entropy from either the resolved binary state (0 or 1) or by measuring the resolving latency T_resolve using a high-precision time-to-digital converter (TDC). Metastability TRNGs offer immense advantages: they can generate true random bits on every single clock edge with minimal dynamic power consumption, making them ideal for battery-powered smart cards and ultra-low-power IoT nodes.
parts.example: Forcing a cross-coupled latch into unstable equilibrium causes it to resolve exponentially (V_diff = V_noise * exp(t/tau)), where the final digital state is dictated by instantaneous thermal noise polarity.
parts.code:
# Day 48 Part 3: Metastable Cross-Coupled Latch Resolution & Latency Entropy Harvester
import struct
import math
import random

class MetastableLatchTRNG:
    """Simulates a cross-coupled bistable latch forced into metastability."""
    def __init__(self, tau_ps: float = 45.0, thermal_sigma_mv: float = 0.85):
        self.tau = tau_ps              # Regeneration time constant in picoseconds
        self.sigma_noise = thermal_sigma_mv  # Thermal noise RMS in millivolts
        self.v_threshold_mv = 500.0   # Digital logic switching threshold in mV

    def trigger_metastable_evaluation(self) -> dict:
        """Releases latch from saddle point and models exponential resolution driven by thermal noise."""
        # Instantaneous thermal noise voltage at resolution release
        v_noise = random.gauss(0.0, self.sigma_noise)
        
        # Prevent division by zero if noise is astronomically close to 0
        if abs(v_noise) < 1.0e-6:
            v_noise = 1.0e-6 if v_noise >= 0 else -1.0e-6

        # Resolved digital state dictated by the sign of the thermal noise
        resolved_bit = 1 if v_noise > 0.0 else 0

        # Resolving latency: T_resolve = tau * ln(V_threshold / |V_noise|)
        t_resolve_ps = self.tau * math.log(self.v_threshold_mv / abs(v_noise))
        t_resolve_ps = max(self.tau, t_resolve_ps)

        return {
            'resolved_bit': resolved_bit,
            'noise_mv': round(v_noise, 4),
            'latency_ps': round(t_resolve_ps, 2)
        }

def run_metastability_trng_demo():
    random.seed(0x5EED4803)
    latch = MetastableLatchTRNG(tau_ps=45.0, thermal_sigma_mv=0.85)
    print("=== Metastability-Based TRNG Latch Resolution Simulation ===")
    print(f"Regeneration Time Constant Tau: {latch.tau} ps | Thermal Noise Sigma: {latch.sigma_noise} mV\n")

    trials = 6
    bits = []
    latencies = []
    for i in range(trials):
        res = latch.trigger_metastable_evaluation()
        bits.append(str(res['resolved_bit']))
        latencies.append(res['latency_ps'])
        print(f"Evaluation {i}: Thermal Noise = {res['noise_mv']:+7.4f} mV | "
              f"Resolve Latency = {res['latency_ps']:6.2f} ps -> Bit = {res['resolved_bit']}")

    print(f"\nHarvested Bit Sequence: {''.join(bits)}")
    print(f"Mean Resolving Latency: {sum(latencies)/len(latencies):.2f} ps")
    print("Metastability Harvester Verdict: SADDLE_POINT_ENTROPY_EXTRACTED")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    run_metastability_trng_demo()

parts.title: Digital Post-Processing & Von Neumann De-Biasing Algorithms
say: Even with the most carefully calibrated physical entropy harvesters, raw digitizer outputs inevitably exhibit subtle physical imperfections: direct-current (DC) voltage offsets in comparators, transistor mismatch in cross-coupled latches, and clock duty-cycle distortion. As a result, raw physical bitstreams typically suffer from Bit Bias (e.g., 51.5% ones and 48.5% zeros) and Temporal Autocorrelation (where bit N correlates slightly with bit N+1).

Under international cryptographic standards (NIST SP 800-90B, BSI AIS-31, FIPS 140-3), raw physical entropy must NEVER be exposed directly to cryptographic consumers. Instead, the raw bitstream must pass through Digital Post-Processing (Conditioning). Conditioning transforms a non-ideal, weakly biased physical entropy source into a cryptographically uniform, uncorrupted random bitstream with maximal Shannon and min-entropy.

The most classical and elegant unbiasing algorithm in computing history is John von Neumann's De-Biasing Algorithm (introduced in 1951). Von Neumann realized that any stationary memoryless binary source with unknown, fixed bias p (where Pr[bit=1] = p and Pr[bit=0] = 1-p) can be converted into a perfectly unbiased source with Pr[bit=1] = 0.5 without knowing the value of p!
The Von Neumann algorithm groups incoming raw bits into non-overlapping consecutive pairs (b_{2i}, b_{2i+1}):
1. If the pair is '01', the algorithm outputs a single bit '0'. The probability of this event is (1-p) * p.
2. If the pair is '10', the algorithm outputs a single bit '1'. The probability of this event is p * (1-p).
3. If the pair is '00' or '11', the pair is completely discarded, and no bit is output.

Notice the mathematical perfection: because Pr['01'] = p*(1-p) and Pr['10'] = (1-p)*p, both events are strictly equiprobable regardless of the bias p! The resulting filtered stream is provably unbiased. The trade-off is variable throughput: the expected output bit yield per raw input bit is p*(1-p) <= 0.25, requiring 4 to 8 raw physical bits to yield a single conditioned bit.

To achieve higher throughput efficiency, advanced implementations employ the Peres De-Biasing Algorithm (introduced by Yuval Peres in 1992). Peres proved that by recursively applying Von Neumann unbiasing to the discarded '00' and '11' pairs (extracting residual entropy from the sum and difference sequences), the extraction efficiency approaches the fundamental Shannon entropy limit H(p) = -p*log2(p) - (1-p)*log2(1-p), asymptotically achieving near-100% extraction efficiency.

Universal Hash Extractors based on Toeplitz Matrix Multiplication provide an information-theoretically secure alternative to cryptographic hashing. A linear feedback shift register parameterized by a public random seed generates a Toeplitz matrix over the finite field GF(2). When a raw physical vector of length N is multiplied by this M x N Toeplitz matrix, the Leftover Hash Lemma guarantees that the M output bits are statistically indistinguishable from a uniform distribution, provided M <= N * H_inf - 2 * log2(1 / epsilon). Unlike block ciphers or hash functions that rely on computational complexity assumptions, universal hash extraction is provably secure against adversaries equipped with infinite computational power.

Under the NIST SP 800-90B framework, the conditioning component must undergo rigorous min-entropy verification. If the raw physical source provides an assessed min-entropy of H_in bits per sample, and the conditioning function has an input length of n_in bits and output length of n_out bits, the standard provides explicit formulas (such as the narrow-pipe and wide-pipe bounds) to calculate the certified output min-entropy H_out. If the entropy margin is insufficient, the architecture must increase the compression ratio (e.g. 4:1 or 8:1) to ensure full-entropy certification.

In modern high-speed security processors, cryptographic conditioning functions are implemented using Linear Feedback Shift Registers (LFSRs) or Cryptographic Hash Functions. The NIST SP 800-90B standard endorses vetted conditioning components such as CBC-MAC, HMAC-SHA256, and AES-based hash extractors. Passing 1,024 raw physical bits with assessed min-entropy of 0.6 bits/bit through SHA-256 compresses 614 bits of physical entropy into a full-entropy 256-bit cryptographic key, satisfying all FIPS 140-3 requirements.

parts.code:
# Day 48 Part 4: Von Neumann De-Biasing Algorithm & NIST SP 800-90B Cryptographic Conditioning
import struct
import hashlib
import random

class VonNeumannDebiaser:
    """Implements John von Neumann's classic unbiasing algorithm for stationary biased sources."""
    @staticmethod
    def process_bitstream(raw_bits: list) -> list:
        """Consumes raw bit pairs: '01' -> 0, '10' -> 1, '00'/'11' -> discard."""
        conditioned_bits = []
        for i in range(0, len(raw_bits) - 1, 2):
            b0, b1 = raw_bits[i], raw_bits[i + 1]
            if b0 == 0 and b1 == 1:
                conditioned_bits.append(0)
            elif b0 == 1 and b1 == 0:
                conditioned_bits.append(1)
            # If b0 == b1: discard
        return conditioned_bits

class NISTConditioningEngine:
    """NIST SP 800-90B Cryptographic Conditioning using SHA-256 compression."""
    @staticmethod
    def condition_raw_entropy(raw_bytes: bytes) -> bytes:
        """Compresses raw physical entropy buffer into full-entropy 256-bit conditioned block."""
        hasher = hashlib.sha256()
        hasher.update(b"NIST_SP800_90B_CONDITIONING_V1")
        hasher.update(raw_bytes)
        return hasher.digest()

def run_debiasing_demonstration():
    random.seed(0x5EED4804)
    # Generate 1,000 bits from a heavily biased physical source (Pr[1] = 0.65)
    bias_p = 0.65
    raw_bits = [1 if random.random() < bias_p else 0 for _ in range(1000)]
    
    raw_ones = raw_bits.count(1)
    print("=== Raw vs Conditioned Entropy De-Biasing Bench ===")
    print(f"Raw Input Stream:     1,000 bits")
    print(f"Raw Physical Bias:    {raw_ones / 10.0:.2f}% Ones (Severe Transistor Mismatch)\n")

    # 1. Apply Von Neumann De-Biasing
    vn_bits = VonNeumannDebiaser.process_bitstream(raw_bits)
    vn_ones = vn_bits.count(1)
    vn_pct = (vn_ones / float(len(vn_bits))) * 100.0 if vn_bits else 0.0
    print(f"Von Neumann Output:   {len(vn_bits)} bits (Efficiency: {len(vn_bits)/10.0:.1f}%)")
    print(f"Conditioned Bias:     {vn_pct:.2f}% Ones (Ideal: 50.0%)")

    # 2. Apply NIST SP 800-90B SHA-256 Conditioning
    raw_byte_data = bytes([sum(raw_bits[i+j] << (7-j) for j in range(8)) for i in range(0, len(raw_bits)-7, 8)])
    conditioned_block = NISTConditioningEngine.condition_raw_entropy(raw_byte_data)
    print(f"\nNIST SP 800-90B 256-bit Block: {conditioned_block.hex()[:32]}...")
    print("Post-Processing Verdict: PERFECT_UNIFORM_ENTROPY_ACHIEVED")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    run_debiasing_demonstration()

By multiplying the incoming bitstream by the square root of the system clock frequency

parts.title: TRNG Microarchitecture & Active Physical Attack Defenses
say: Building a mathematically sound TRNG in simulation is only half the battle; the true crucible for hardware security architects is defending physical TRNG silicon against Active Physical Attacks.

In commercial high-assurance environments--such as automotive gateways, banking chips, and defense crypto modules--the TRNG is under constant threat from physical adversaries seeking to manipulate the physical environment to collapse entropy. The three primary physical attack vectors against TRNGs are:

1. Frequency Injection Locking: An adversary couples an external high-power radio-frequency (RF) signal or alternating magnetic field into the silicon die via the package pins or localized EM probes. If the RF frequency matches the ring oscillator's resonance frequency, the oscillator injection-locks, synchronizing its switching to the external clock. Phase jitter collapses to zero, and the TRNG outputs an entirely predictable bit pattern.

2. Temperature Freezing / Clamping: An attacker cools the microchip to sub-zero temperatures (-40C or liquid nitrogen at -196C) using Peltier coolers or cryogenic sprays. As temperature drops toward absolute zero, Johnson-Nyquist thermal noise V_rms = sqrt(4 * k_B * T * R * Delta_f) drops dramatically, suppressing the primary physical entropy source and starving the harvester.

3. Power Supply Ripple & Fault Injection: By superimposing high-frequency sine waves onto the Vdd core voltage rail, an attacker induces deterministic jitter patterns across all ring oscillators simultaneously, creating correlated bit sequences.

To defeat these physical attacks, modern secure TRNG microarchitectures integrate dedicated On-Chip Active Health Tests mandated by NIST SP 800-90B and BSI AIS-31 PTG.2. These include Repetition Count Tests (detecting if the harvester is stuck on a constant 0 or 1), Adaptive Proportion Tests (detecting sudden bias shifts within a sliding window of 512 or 1024 samples), and Frequency Spread Monitors.

Furthermore, hardened physical designs deploy Differential Ring Oscillators (cross-coupled delay lines that reject common-mode supply noise), on-chip temperature freeze sensors that shut down the TRNG if temperatures drop below -30C, and hardware zeroization strobes that wipe all key buffers the instant an active attack is detected.

Silicon layout defenses are equally vital: layout engineers place continuous active top-metal shield meshes above all TRNG analog cells and ring oscillators, carrying high-frequency pseudorandom dynamic signals. If an attacker drills into the package to insert microprobes or focus laser beams onto the ring oscillators, cutting the shield triggers an instantaneous hardware security reset.

Finally, under FIPS 140-3 Level 4 and Common Criteria EAL6+ certification requirements, if any online health test fails, the TRNG must inhibit all random bit output within 1 clock cycle, assert an unmaskable hardware tamper interrupt to the Root of Trust security co-processor, and zeroize the internal DRBG state registers to prevent stale or deterministic entropy consumption.

In addition to runtime tests, high-assurance silicon incorporates Startup Health Tests (mandated by NIST SP 800-90B Section 4.3). Prior to generating the very first cryptographic nonce or key upon boot, the TRNG collects an initial batch of 4,096 raw physical bits and runs full battery tests, including Repetition Count, Adaptive Proportion, and Chi-Squared goodness-of-fit tests. Only after the initial 4,096 bits pass all statistical thresholds does the hardware assert the ENTROPY_READY flag, releasing the system reset to the primary application core.

Differential power analysis (DPA) defenses must also surround the TRNG digitizer and conditioning logic. When ring oscillators transition, their dynamic switching current I_dd = C_pd * Vdd * f creates detectable electromagnetic emissions on the power pins. If an attacker can measure the instantaneous current of individual oscillators, they can reconstruct the raw jitter trajectory before XOR reduction. Secure implementations deploy on-chip Low-Dropout (LDO) regulators with high power-supply rejection ratios (PSRR > 60 dB) dedicated exclusively to the TRNG domain, alongside current-flattening dummy load circuits that ensure constant aggregate power draw.
In Part 5, we build a complete active TRNG defense controller integrating raw physical jitter sampling, on-the-fly health monitoring, injection-locking detection, and autonomous circuit shutdown.

parts.code:
# Day 48 Part 5: Hardened TRNG Microarchitecture with Active Attack Detection & NIST Health Monitor
import struct
import random

class HardenedTRNGController:
    """Industrial TRNG controller with on-chip NIST SP 800-90B real-time health monitors."""
    def __init__(self, repetition_cutoff: int = 12, adaptive_window: int = 512, adaptive_cutoff: int = 320):
        self.rep_cutoff = repetition_cutoff        # Repetition Count Test threshold
        self.window_size = adaptive_window         # Adaptive Proportion Test window
        self.adapt_cutoff = adaptive_cutoff        # Max allowed count of most common bit
        
        self.history = []
        self.last_bit = None
        self.consecutive_count = 0
        self.tamper_alert_latched = False

    def monitor_sample(self, bit: int) -> bool:
        """Runs NIST SP 800-90B continuous health tests. Returns False and latches alert if failed."""
        if self.tamper_alert_latched:
            return False  # Hardware remains shut down until full secure reset

        # 1. Repetition Count Test
        if bit == self.last_bit:
            self.consecutive_count += 1
            if self.consecutive_count >= self.rep_cutoff:
                self.tamper_alert_latched = True
                print(f"[CRITICAL_ALERT] Repetition Count Violation: {self.consecutive_count} consecutive {bit}s!")
                return False
        else:
            self.last_bit = bit
            self.consecutive_count = 1

        # 2. Adaptive Proportion Test over sliding window
        self.history.append(bit)
        if len(self.history) > self.window_size:
            self.history.pop(0)

        if len(self.history) == self.window_size:
            count_ones = sum(self.history)
            max_count = max(count_ones, self.window_size - count_ones)
            if max_count >= self.adapt_cutoff:
                self.tamper_alert_latched = True
                print(f"[CRITICAL_ALERT] Adaptive Proportion Violation: {max_count}/{self.window_size} identical bits!")
                return False

        return True

def run_hardened_trng_security_test():
    random.seed(0x5EED4805)
    controller = HardenedTRNGController()
    print("=== Hardened TRNG Active Attack Monitoring Bench ===")
    
    # Phase 1: Normal operational jitter stream (healthy)
    print("Phase 1: Evaluating normal healthy physical entropy stream (300 bits)...")
    for _ in range(300):
        bit = 1 if random.random() < 0.51 else 0
        assert controller.monitor_sample(bit) == True
    print("Phase 1 Result: All 300 samples PASSED continuous health tests.")

    # Phase 2: Simulate Active RF Injection Locking (forcing constant '1's)
    print("\nPhase 2: Adversary initiates Active RF Injection Attack (forcing locked '1's)...")
    attack_detected = False
    for cycle in range(20):
        injected_bit = 1  # Attacker locks oscillator
        healthy = controller.monitor_sample(injected_bit)
        if not healthy:
            print(f"Cycle {cycle+1}: TRNG Hardware Intercepted Attack! Latched Secure Lockout.")
            attack_detected = True
            break

    print(f"\nHardened TRNG Defense Verdict: {'ACTIVE_INJECTION_CONTAINED_TRNG_LOCKED' if attack_detected else 'FAILED'}")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    run_hardened_trng_security_test()

summary: Hardware TRNGs harvest non-deterministic physical entropy from microscopic thermal Johnson-Nyquist noise, quantum shot noise, and transistor switching jitter.
Free-running Ring Oscillators accumulate phase jitter as an unconstrained random walk (sigma proportional to sqrt(t)), yielding uniform phase uncertainty when sampled by a reference clock.
Metastable cross-coupled latches amplify microscopic sub-millivolt thermal noise exponentially, resolving into logic 0 or 1 based on the instantaneous noise polarity.
Von Neumann de-biasing mathematically cancels stationary physical bias by pairing bits (01->0, 10->1), followed by cryptographic conditioning to ensure full-entropy output.
NIST SP 800-90B continuous health tests (Repetition Count Test and Adaptive Proportion Test) protect silicon against active RF injection locking and temperature clamping attacks.
